utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in court today. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP, everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for General Delic. Lana Deljkic is our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. May the witness please make the declaration. Will you please stand up, sir. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may now be seated. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Menon will be leading this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: My name is Izudin Hajderhodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you please state your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Twenty-third of May, 1947, and the place is Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hajderhodzic, can you please identify the positions that you held in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the time periods in which you held those positions?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The BH Army officially came into existence in 1993, when the brigades were set up, when the army was officially set up. Before that, there used to be the TO, which existed between April and 1992 [as interpreted]. From April 1992 to 1997, I was an operative officer at the town command. After that, I was an operative officer with the 318th Mountain Brigade. After that, I was assistant commander for Intelligence in the 318th Mountain Brigade. After that, I was a desk officer for Intelligence in the Bosnian Operations Group, which later became the 55th Division -- 35th Division. I kept my position in the 35th Division, and several months after it was set up, I became assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division, and I remained in that position until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, it says, in your answer, it says: "From April 1992 to 1997, I was an operative officer at the town command." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Between April 1992 and the start of 1993, which means throughout 1992, at the time the BH Army was not yet in existence because the units had not yet been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then you refer to your being an operative officer with the 318th Brigade and the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 318th Mountain Brigade, a desk officer for Intelligence in the Bosnian Operations Group, and later the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division. Do you recall the time periods in which you occupied each of these positions?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't have a very good head for dates. I can't remember every single appointment, but I do remember the events well. When the 320th Brigade was set up in Zavidovici, there was a great shuffle, and the Bosnia OG was there, and the 320th Brigade was set up, and it was at that time that I switched to the OG. The OG, however, soon evolved into a division, and this all happened over a time period of mere months. I can't remember the exact date. I really have difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, sir. But can you tell me what position -- of the positions that you've referred to, which position did you occupy in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: 1995, I was assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And I'd like to focus on your position as the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 35th Division. Can you tell us what the focus of the 35th Division's intelligence department was, what the focus of its work was?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The focus of the work of the assistant commander for Intelligence, not just in the 35th Division, was to gather intelligence on the enemy. Assistant commanders for Intelligence were meant to gather intelligence on the enemy facing us, each in our own areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And by what means would the intelligence department acquire information on the enemy?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Information was acquired in a peculiar way, given the nature of our situation. We organised ourselves in such a manner that we had intelligence bodies up to battalion level. We had those in divisions, in brigades and in battalions. Those were men who were, in a way, subordinated to the intelligence body of the 35th Division. How was information acquired? There were different ways. We used whatever we could. We carried out reconnaissance. We used surveillance. We watched TV stations. We listened to radio stations. We tried to intercept enemy communications via counter-electronic equipment. And if any prisoners were taken, we tried to get that type of information, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Can you describe how the intelligence department of the 35th Division was organised, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: There were three men working there, me and two clerical officers who were in charge of this, and then there was the POW -- PEB department which normally numbered between 10 and 20 men. That was as far as the division was concerned. Obviously, we also had units and assistant commanders for Intelligence in lower-level units at battalion commands, brigade commands, who would submit information to us regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, you referred to a PEB department. Can you tell us what the function of that department was?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to listen to everything that was being emitted, everything that was on air, as it were, all the information that was being exchanged by the enemy, in a bit, to learn as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom did the leader of this particular department report, the PEB department?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The PEB commander was subordinated to the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division, which means me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, as the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 35th Division, from whom did you receive your orders?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The intelligence organ had two chains of commanders, a horizontal one and a vertical one. Technical issues had to do with the corps, and horizontally speaking, the commander was the commander of the 35th Division. My commander was the commander of the 35th Division. I could put it like that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you referred to the corps. Did you have a superior in the corps?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The assistant commander for Intelligence of the corps was my direct superior, in purely professional and technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain, would there be a difference in the subject matter over which -- over which the corps would have authority over you, vis a vis the 35th Division commander?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I hope I understand your question correctly. My commander was the commander of the 35th Division. Any tasks that I carried out, any information that I obtained, I would write down and submit directly to the corps, always to the commander of the 35th Division. The commander of the 35th Division never, and that was precisely the way it was supposed to be, tried to alter any of the my reports or influence me in any way in the production of these reports, but he did look at each and every one of the reports that I produced. Any orders from the corps, sometimes issued by the assistant commander, instructions and so on and so forth, would always go through the commander, and the commander always knew exactly what sort of orders I was receiving. This was necessary for him to supervise my work, because he was responsible for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in your answer, you state that "any orders from the corps issued by the assistant commander, instructions and so on and so forth, would always go through the commander." When you say "the commander," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I mean the commander of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when the commander of the 35th Division would issue orders to you, would those orders go through the corps, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, those didn't go through the corps. There was a direct line. At any rate, it was somehow always my responsibility to inform about whatever orders I may have received. Of course, this only applies to situations where any orders that I received were contrary to the nature of my job and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow your intercourse with the witness, and I'm getting lost. First, at page 6, lines 16 to 17, he says: "I would write down and submit directly to the corps, always to the commander of the 35th Division." That sounds to be self-contradictory. Is it directly to the corps or to the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was actually going to clarify the reporting structure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I've been waiting for you to do so. That's why I didn't intervene immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in any case, some of the explanations that you have been getting after that confuse me even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try and clarify the reporting structure, and hopefully the other matters will become a little clearer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, you've touched upon how you reported to your superiors. Can you describe -- can you describe further how you would submit a report to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to provide a more comprehensive explanation, and I'm about to tell you why. The 35th Division would send out three parallel reports, an operative report, an intelligence report and a security report. All of these three reports would be sent to the corps. The operative report was drafted based on all these reports, and this was the commander's report. He was meant to have all information from the intelligence organ, from the security organ, and he would produce his report based on those sources. Therefore, before the commander does his job, I first submit a report to the intelligence body, or rather I have to finish it and then I have to submit it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, we have to interrupt you. When you keep saying "commander," I'm not sure whether you're talking about the commander of the 35th Division or the commander of the corps, so can you please explain at each time which commander you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "the commander," I always mean the commander of the 35th Division, because that is the highest level that I will be talking about. The next command higher up is not a command that I can comment on or that I am particularly knowledgeable about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, can you continue with your answer?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I had to submit my report by -- I'm not sure exactly what time, but half an hour before the operative report. The operative report would include part of my own reports. The operatives would include whatever they saw fit, whatever they deemed necessary. My report, being what it was, based on what I had previously received and the way I signed it off, would then be submitted directly to the corps. No one from the Command of the 35th Division never tried to alter or, indeed, altered any of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, to whom in the corps would your report be directed?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: My report was addressed to the intelligence organ of the 35th -- the 33rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to the 33rd Corps. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry. 3rd Corps. I may be slightly confused, so sometimes I misspeak. The 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, the report that you sent to the 3rd Corps, would that be different -- the intelligence department of the 3rd Corps, would be different from the report that you sent to the commander of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, it was exactly the same. It was submitted for inspection to the commander of the 35th Division. The original, on the other hand, was submitted directly to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how frequently would you send such reports, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: As a rule, these reports were produced on a daily basis. These were daily reports, therefore. They would normally be dispatched in the evening hours, but sometimes there were interim reports that were dispatched at any time that the situation called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And beyond written reports, were there any other means by which you reported to the 35th Division commander and the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The meetings at the 3rd Corps were not exactly regular, but they would be held sometimes in the intelligence offices of the intelligence organ. We would meet once every two months or so and discuss matters. This was more in order to get to know each other better and to receive further instructions. Those weren't frequent meetings, and I was not directly in touch with the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 3rd Corps. We only ever communicated via reports and by telephone. There was a period in time -- actually, throughout 1995 we always spoke on the phone. As for communication, as for contacts with the commander of the 35th Division or the Command of the 35th Division, in peace-time conditions, conditionally speaking, and by this I mean when there were no combat operations in progress, we would have regular meetings every morning, brief meetings, everyone said whatever it was that they had to say, and then we would all be off on our different jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, while you were the assistant commander for Intelligence in the 35th Division, who was the commander of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The division commander was Mr. Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was your superior in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps, Edin Husic, Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And just for clarification, what was Mr. Edin Husic's position?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Edin Husic was assistant commander for Intelligence of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, can you describe how the -- how the intelligence departments were organised at the brigade level, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, any brigade would have an assistant commander for Intelligence. The assistant commander would have one or two desk officers, depending on the brigade and depending on the brigade's position and assignment. And in lower-level units such as battalions, again there were assistant commanders for Intelligence. There would be two or three men at brigade level, and each battalion would have another one or two. Under the commander of the assistant commander for Intelligence, as a rule -- well, not exactly always, but most frequently there would be a squad or a platoon of scouts, intelligence scouts. So that would be the structure of a brigade intelligence organ for you, in very rough terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, in your last answer, you said: "under the commander of the assistant commander of Intelligence, as a rule -- well, not exactly, but most frequently there would be a squad or a platoon of scouts." Which assistant commander for Intelligence are you referring to, at which level are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I mean the assistant commander for Intelligence of the brigade, because we started speaking about the brigade two minutes ago, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And now to whom would the assistant commander for Intelligence at the brigade level report?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The chain of command in the BH Army was the same. From battalion level to the very top -- well, I myself know about the division, but he was subordinated to the brigade commander, and in professional and technical terms also to the assistant commander for Intelligence of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, in your last answer, you referred to the battalion level. I asked you at the brigade level, to whom would the assistant commander for Intelligence at the brigade level report?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I was speaking about the brigade. I may have misspoken if I said "battalion." But assistant commander for Intelligence, the brigade assistant commander, was subordinated to the brigade commander and, in technical terms, to the assistant commander for Intelligence of the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "technical terms," what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: These are peculiar tasks, and the commander is responsible for the entire military formation that he's in charge of and the way it is organised. There are various bodies working there, and this is something that is very peculiar, unique if you like, and so are all the other sectors. Therefore, there had to be some link running down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say, "the commander is responsible for the entire military formation," which commander are you referring to and at which level?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, all commanders are responsible for their units at their level. That's what they're there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the brigade -- the assistant commander for Intelligence at the brigade level, who was -- who was subordinated to the assistant commander for Intelligence at the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: At the brigade level, the scouts squad or platoon was subordinates, at the brigade level, and the assistant commanders for Intelligence in battalions, so their number depended on the number of battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, in an earlier answer, sir, you had indicated that one of the sources of information, intelligence information, was -- were through prisoners of war. In the context of a combat operation, how was the -- how would the processing of a prisoner of war be regulated?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Every activity is documented, and for every activity the procedure -- the treatment of prisoners is strictly stipulated, and this is regulated in an order issued by the person who is responsible for treating the prisoners, how to do that, in what manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02264. Oh, I'm sorry, I was told that it's Exhibit 444. I'd still like the witness to look at it, though. And if we could go to page 34 of the English and page -- well, actually, if we could just stay on page one and I'll ask the witness a question, and then if we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: To what combat operation does this document relate?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Order for the continuation of the attack Proljece-1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to page 34 of the English and page 34 of the B/C/S. And I would note, for the record, that this document is dated the 18th of July, 1995. If we could scroll up on the English. And if we could go to page 13 of the B/C/S. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the section labelled 16.12, "Procedures with Prisoners of War." Can you read that section to yourself? Sir, which organs of the 35th Division does this provision apply to?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: These provisions apply to, as indicated quite clearly here, to the intelligence and security organ, so two sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in light of this provision, what would the responsibilities of the 35th Division's intelligence department be in relation to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The intelligence sector did not have any jurisdiction, at least not as far as the prisoners of war were concerned, except in terms of gathering any information that those prisoners might provide. Everything else was in the purview of the security organ. The security organ had the capability to receive, transport and ensure the security of the prisoners of war. The intelligence organ's only role was to try and find out -- try and learn as much as possible from the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when would the -- generally speaking, when would the intelligence department make contact with a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: As a rule, immediately, as soon as the prisoners are taken, because that's when you can get some information, perhaps, and this information is quite important and the information is valid for a short period of time. This is especially the case when you have a combat situation which is developing very quickly. And this information is not so important, after all. You always have to make that assessment, and that's what we always did, whether we should interview the prisoners or not. But in this order, it is stipulated that the intelligence and security organs are actually given the right -- I am given the right to approach the prisoner and to talk to those prisoners, but I am not under any obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "and this information is not so important, after all," can you explain why you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: If a combat engagement is going on, the situation changes from one moment to the next, and the situation as it was ten minutes ago, it just is not like that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us what kind of information you would solicit from a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, our units sought to confirm -- I sought to confirm who these people were, who it was that we faced, because units would switch, would be rotated on the front lines, and any other information that could be obtained from those prisoners. That would not be much, because these people, for the most part, didn't really have that much knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the information that you received from a prisoner of war, what would you do with that information?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, whatever the information was that I received, I would type it up and send it onwards, with a comment on my part. This was raw intelligence, so I would send it on to the 3rd Corps, to my professional and technical superior in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, again, to whom in the 3rd Corps would you send that information?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, I avoid naming names, because it could have been anyone, but that would always be the assistant commander for Intelligence. In this case, it was Edin Husic, but it could have been any other person, because names are not relevant here. The important thing is the function, the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And would you report that information to your other superior, the 35th Division commander?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already indicated that all the reports that were sent to the corps were first given to the commander of the 31st [as interpreted] division for his information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And would you ever give information to the -- and you refer to the 31st Division, sir. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken, but it's the 35th Division. Well, it's always the 35th Division and the 3rd Corps, so even if -- and the brigades that were subordinate to them. I am not going to be referring to any other units, or I will do so very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, would you ever transmit information to the 35th Division commander without reporting that to the assistant commander for Intelligence at the 3rd Corps level?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: You asked me if I would have sent it to the assistant commander for Intelligence at the 3rd Corps without informing the division commander? I don't know if I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was actually the other way around. Would you ever report information to the 35th Division commander without reporting that same information to the assistant commander for Intelligence at the 3rd Corps level?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, never. Everything that was done in writing would be sent to the commander of the 35th Division and the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for that clarification. Now, sir, do you recall if any prisoners of war were taken during the Proljece-95 operation?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the first prisoners of war that we took. Yes, there were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how were you informed of their capture?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know where I was at that time, but somebody called me on the phone and told me that they had been captured and that I should go to Zavidovici and that I should meet up with the assistant commander for Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where were you when you received this telephone call, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when, in relation to the combat operations, did you receive this telephone call, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I said I don't recall where I was at the time, but I was somewhere on the front line. I really can't recall where I was, because there were so many things, I can't really remember where I was. But at any rate, I was at a place where I could be reached by phone. There weren't so many places like that, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, you referred to the assistant commander for Security. Does this person have a name?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the assistant commander for Security in the 35th Division was a man by the name of Fadil Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the prisoners of war, when you found out about their capture, where were they being held, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was contained in the first report that I received, but I know that there were some prisoners of war and that we were supposed to meet in Zavidovici, to go and have a look at those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where did you go in order to meet those prisoners, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: We went to the village of Livade. It is in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division, and it's in the immediate vicinity of Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "we," who are you referring to, for clarification?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I am referring to Mr. Imamovic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Livade, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Since we didn't know where the prisoners were, we asked around. I don't know who it was that we asked, and that person told us that we should ask an Arab who was down there. We tried to get in touch with him. It was difficult because the man had difficulty speaking. It was hard for us to understand each other. And when we told him that we wanted to see the prisoners, he first objected. He didn't want us to look at them. And then he asked somebody -- I don't know who it was. He went down further into the village of Livade. He came back and he said that we could see them, but for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who first informed you -- who first directed you to the Arab?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was, but one of those persons who were present there, who were milling around that area. There were civilians, soldiers. I really don't know who it was who told us to do that, but that's an area which is maybe 50 to 100 metres in size. It's a small village. The distances are not that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know to whom the Arab spoke to before giving you permission to meet the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I didn't see that man. I know that he spoke to somebody down there and that then he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when the Arab came back, where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: He took us to a house which was very close by. He took us up an outdoor staircase into a corridor, and he took us into an empty room to the left of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when he took you into this room, what happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: He said that we should wait a while. He went out, and then we heard voices outside. I didn't understand what they were saying. After a while -- in fact, first he asked us, "Who do you want us, who do you want me to bring you," and he gave us some names that didn't mean anything to us. And he said that there was a doctor among them, and we agreed that he should bring in the doctor because we didn't know who the others were, and we assumed that the doctor would be a person that we could talk to. He went back out, and we heard the voices, and after a while they brought this man in, into this room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know from where they brought this man in?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, but I assume that he had been in one of those rooms that you could get in from that same corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you -- when you say "they brought this man in," who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how many Arabs, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe how the prisoner was brought in?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: He was carried in. They carried him in. He was tied to a pole. And then they put it down on the floor. There was no furniture in this room. We didn't have anything to sit on. It was empty. So we just stood there. I don't remember what exactly it looked like. But at any rate, he was carried in and then they dropped him onto the floor. He was tied to this pole with some wire. It was a nasty sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What part of his body was tied to the pole, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Both his hands and his feet. The pole went below his knees and above his elbows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, did this prisoner speak to you?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't really recall, because the moment I saw what this man looked like and the way he was tied up, you can't talk to a man like that, so I don't remember what the conversation was like. And even if we did talk to him, we asked him for his name, who he was, where he was from, but we didn't talk to him any further. There was no need for us to talk to him. This would have been in vain. We couldn't really ask this man anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you take any steps to try and -- to try and have the man's situation corrected at that -- at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that both of us demanded that the man's hands be untied, but it was impossible because his hands were all blue. We wanted his hands to be untied, at least, but the Arab would not allow that and he didn't, in fact, allow us to discuss this issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, were you familiar -- before this incident, were you familiar with how a prisoner of war was to be treated?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, we should all know how prisoners of war are to be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did what you see comport with the appropriate treatment for a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in line with those regulations, but my human feelings were against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, you've touched upon it briefly, but can you recall what you asked, if anything, of the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what I asked him or whether I asked him anything. If I did, I asked him just the basic information; name, his affiliation, what unit he was in, because you cannot really ask any questions of a man in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you recall if Mr. Imamovic asked any questions of the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, when I said I or Imamovic, I think that we both asked the same questions, and I think that Imamovic shared my feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, how long did this encounter with this prisoner last, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: It was a very brief encounter. I don't really know. But what I wanted was to get out of there as soon as possible. Well, I can't now tell you how many minutes we were there or anything, but it was a very, very brief period of time, because especially as I sit here, I cannot tell you how long we spent there, but it was a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you recall if Mr. Imamovic was with you during the entire duration that you were in the house?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. We kept to each other's sides at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt before we do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, did you come to know the names of the two Arabs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you come to know the name of the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned the name of the prisoner afterwards, or rather I knew his name right there, I learnt it there, and I wrote it down in my notebook. This is something that one tends to forget, and once you write it down and once you send it on, then it is recorded. This was the first and the last time that I saw those Arabs. I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember the name of the prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that he's a doctor, but I would never be able to remember that. I know that his name is Sikiric, but I had to look it up in my notebook. There were some conversations later on in Sarajevo, and that's why I remember it. Otherwise, I would not have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sikanic, but I'm not quite sure, actually, what his name is exactly, but that would be the general idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You wanted the witness to see P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you talk to other of the prisoners or did you only see Dr. Sikanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember only Dr. Sikanic. I don't remember anyone else. I don't know. There are two other names in my notebook, and I don't know why they're there. I don't remember any other prisoners. I simply don't have any recollection of them. And if you were to ask me what this Dr. Sikanic looked like, I couldn't tell you. I don't know. I couldn't describe him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P02288. And I'll just note the document is dated the 22nd of July, 1995. And if we could go to page 2 of the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you read the second sentence of the second paragraph to yourself, and that would be the second sentence of the first paragraph in the English. Have you had a chance to read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which one you mean exactly. Ask the question and I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just scroll down for a second in the B/C/S version. I guess we're down as far as -- sir, can you make out who signed this document? And if we could focus in on the signature?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to read. Yes, Fadil Imamovic. It's faintly legible. And the header reads that this is a document by the Security Service, so if this was the Security Service, then this should be assistant commander for Security, Fadil Imamovic. That is precisely what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And this was the person that accompanied you to Livade; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could scroll up on the B/C/S version of the document and the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to refer you to the second paragraph, the second sentence of the second paragraph on this page. In that sentence -- in that sentence, there's a reference to "intelligence operative of the 35th Division." To whom does that refer?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: You mean the operative officer? You mean the second sentence: "The interview was conducted at the reception centre in the village of Livade. The interview was conducted with the approval of Abu Maali with the Chetnik prisoners and this --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I misspoke. It's actually the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: All right, sorry, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the interview with the captured Chetniks, and I just want to know to whom does -- it says "the intelligence operative of the 35th Division," I want to know to whom does that refer?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: That's a reference to me, the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division, and it's probably a reference to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And now that same sentence says: "The interview with the captured Chetnik soldiers ..." Can you explain why this document refers to an interview with more than one soldier?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You see, there are three names here. Again, I must say I simply don't remember these two. I don't know whether I saw them or not. This is not something that I remember. I have an informal notebook as well which reflects three names, and they are the same names as the one we see here. That is probably why the plural is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you explain why Mr. Imamovic produced this document?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Imamovic produced this document because it was his responsibility to do so. This was in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. The security organ is responsible for anything that happens in its area of responsibility in terms of security. It is also responsible for POWs. Anything that happens in the area under our control was the responsibility of the security organ, and the intelligence organ was responsible for anything that was happening beyond that area, for information that could be obtained in relation to what was going on on the other side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, does this document refer to your encounter and Mr. Imamovic's encounter with the prisoners in Livade?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And can you -- do you have any explanation for how these other two names were acquired by Mr. Imamovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the witness has told us he does not remember. He's got the names in his book, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. I'll ask now that this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 553.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, what did you do -- after you left -- after leaving the house in Livade, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I know we went back to Zavidovici. After that, I went away because the activities were still ongoing. Therefore, I still had plenty of commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you report the information that you had seen in Livade to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: As we speak, I don't remember whether I actually submitted a written report or not. It was my responsibility to submit one whenever I had information that had to do with my work. Right now, I can't state with certainty whether, in fact, I did submit a written report on this occasion or not. Previously, yes, I remember submitting one, and I know why. Because in that notebook, I found the names, and next to the names the remark: "They know nothing." So I'm not sure if I actually submitted a report in writing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "previously, yes, I remember submitting one," can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: You'll have to remind me. Did I say that I had, in fact, submitted a report? I believe I said I wasn't sure whether, in fact, I submitted a report or not. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm reading from the transcript from the previous answer that you had given, and you said: "Right now, I can't state with certainty whether, in fact, I did submit a written report on this occasion or not. Previously, yes, I remember submitting one, and I know why." And I was just wondering if you could clarify that answer further.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: My answer is as follows: I don't remember whether I submitted a report or not. My responsibility would have been, if there was any sort of intelligence whatsoever available to me, to produce and submit this report. Since there was no intelligence that was particularly interesting, that was available to me at the time, I'm just not certain that I in fact produced this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the French interpretation of your first answer, we see exactly the same answer that the witness has just provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall informing anybody about the situation in which you had found the prisoner that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: If the situation had been peaceful, if there had been no combat operations in progress, if there had been no activities in progress, I'm certain that I would have reported this at our regular briefings. As it is, I no longer know I told them about the situation in which I found that man in informal communication, and I don't remember exactly who I talked to, but I'm not even sure if I was able to actually see my commander and talk to him at the time. I don't know where he was. I hardly remember where I was. There were combat operations in progress. We were all in different places, each doing our job. At this point in time, I'm pretty certain that I wasn't able to get in touch with any of my superiors which would have enabled me to at least submit an oral report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, for clarification, when you say "superiors," can you just, again for clarification, inform us of whom your superiors were?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: My superior was the commander of the 35th Division, and of course technically Edin Husic, the assistant commander of the 3rd Corps for Intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take note of the time. I do have another document to show the witness that might take some time, and so I can certainly bring it up and start asking him questions, but I would -- in order to finish with that document, I would go over the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want us to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break now and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02317. And I would just note for the record that this document is dated the 24th of July, 1995. If we could go to page 4 of the English and scroll down to the bottom of the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, who is this document signed by?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Captain Abdullah -- there's the signature down there. Captain Sejfulah Mrkaljevic was the desk officer in the Intelligence sector of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to object. This is the second time that the Prosecutor is showing the witness a document, asking him who signed the document, although it is obvious that there is no actual signature. Maybe they should use the expression, "Whose name can we see there?" This document was not signed by hand, and I think it would be a good idea for the record to reflect the fact. If we call these documents signed, that might be misleading, because as a matter of fact they are not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind, Your Honour, and I'll rephrase my questions appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, who was Mr. Mrkaljevic's superior?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for Intelligence, Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 1 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S, and actually scroll up on the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to whom is this document addressed, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: To the forward command post of the 3rd Corps, to Edin Husic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if you could read the first sentence of the first paragraph to yourself, sir. Sir, have you had a chance to read that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There's a reference there to the 35th DKoV PK for ObP. To whom does that refer?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: PK for ObP, assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division, and this refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. If we could go to page 3 of the English, and scroll down on the B/C/S version of the document. If we could go down a bit more on the English version of the document. Sir, I'd like to refer you to the second-to-last paragraph. Can you read that paragraph to yourself, and also the second bullet point which appears underneath it? And this is the last paragraph, Your Honours, on the English version of the document, which follows also the two bullet points. Sir, have you had a chance to read the text that I referred you to? In the first sentence of that paragraph, there's a reference to the briefing of the PK for ObP, and in the second bullet point there's a reference to prisoners from the Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade being held at the El Mujahedin Detachment camp. Do you know how that information reached Mr. Mrkaljevic?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: No. I can hardly comment on this report or any other document produced by my superior command. I would normally never see or receive these documents. As for the first passage, the fact was when somebody was coming to the area of responsibility of the division in which I was the assistant commander for Intelligence, someone from the superior command, my responsibility was to welcome them and to make sure their work was smooth, to make sure they were able to complete all of their assignments, because they always had assignments whenever they came. I made sure that they could do their work. And this document here refers to certain activities which I was unaware of. Particularly, I knew nothing about the prisoners that he refers to, the prisoners of the El Mudjahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know why, in this document, the prisoners held in the El Mujahid Detachment camp at Kamenica, why these prisoners are referred to as being prisoners of the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why they are defined as people who used to be fighters of the 1st Prnjavor Light Brigade. It's difficult to say. I can't speak about this. I only heard of the camp later on. At the time, I was not aware of its existence. I knew that there were some Arabs, or rather -- around. I'm not sure if they were organised into some sort of an army or something. I certainly wasn't aware of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But did you consider the El Mujahid Detachment as being part of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The El Mudjahedin Detachment, in my opinion, was never part of the 35th Division. I didn't know, at the time, anything about its structure, organisation, or anything else. If you just look at this document, I don't even know what date this is, but it doesn't really matter. If someone is a member of the 35th Division, and that unit is superior to another unit, then this someone should know his command. If Mr. Imamovic and I went to Livade, how is it possible, then, for our subordinates not to know us? We were, after all, assistant commanders of the division commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, a division is a big unit, and so maybe not everybody is completely familiar with the leadership of that division. I have no knowledge of why it could be that the people did not recognise you, but I certainly do have a question relating to the fact that you actually went to see the prisoners in Livade and that you apparently accepted that these prisoners were in the hands of the Arabs, as you called them. So you must have considered somehow the relations between the 35th Division and the El Mujahid Detachment, and so I'm curious to know just how you viewed that relation. They couldn't be completely independent, could they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't in the nature of my job to, necessarily, be in contact with them. It wasn't my job, in terms of how the whole thing was organised. Those who could possibly have been in touch with them were other operatives, or security officers, or anyone else, but it certainly wasn't me. The fact is I never considered them a unit that was part of the 35th Division. And until recently, I remain convinced that they were never a part of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, sir, if they were not part of the 35th Division, how could you possibly have accepted that within the area of responsibility of the 35th Division, there certainly was a completely strange and foreign unit that apparently was acting independently of the 35th Division's control? You must have thought that this was strange or somehow sought to ensure that the prisoners would be taken under the proper control of the 35th Division, rather than just leaving them to the fate of some unknown person. You were a responsible officer, and you were aware of the rules, so what did you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a while ago, I worked with an intelligence organ. It was the Security Service that was in charge of security and everything else, and it was their job to deal with everything that was going on within the area of responsibility of the 35th Division; not just the 35th Division, any unit, as a matter of fact, in its area of responsibility. It's the Security Service that must ensure good conditions for everyone's work and for all the activities to run smoothly. My responsibility was different altogether. I believed that since I was with the assistant commander for Security, all of this would eventually be done, and that's all I wanted to know about. I had other objectives, other goals, other jobs, and all of those were catching up with me. I was busy doing something else. As for this order, a while ago I commented on this order for combat operations. It says that the intelligence organ and the security organ have to deal with prisoners, and I told you exactly in what sense. All I was entitled to do is to go and see those prisoners and talk to them, but that was as far as it went. I had no unit under my control that I could possibly have used to do anything at all about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we know that you were not in charge of the prisoners, their condition, the treatment they were receiving, or anything like that. You were merely in charge of questioning them in order to try and find out anything that might be useful by way of information on the enemy. Anyway, how could you have taken this decision to go to Livade in order to interview the prisoners there? How could that have been your objective if the prisoners were not under your control to begin with? If they were not under your control, then probably you were not entitled to go there to begin with; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I didn't even know -- I'm not sure today whether I knew or not that they were in Livade and who they were being held by. It was only after I arrived there that I was certain of this, and then I was able to talk to them. The fact is they were in our area of responsibility. I would see people in the streets sometimes, I would hear things about this being there. Look, I did hear of the existence of some units, but when I say "unit," I know all about all the other units. I know who their commanders are, I know who the command is, I know who does what. After all, I know some individuals as well. And this was a place where I knew no one at all. I didn't know them. I didn't see anyone being lined up. I didn't realise even that this was a separate unit or what they were doing. I really don't know. That's why I can't accept this. I can't accept the hypothesis that they were under the command of the 35th Division, or perhaps I should express the following reservation: They may have been, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, would you have agreed to get in touch with them so that they might provide you with some information? Would you have agreed to hear them out, hear what they had to say, because this is a very unusual situation, the fact that you accepted to get in touch with these people who you saw in the street and no more, as you said; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My job was my job. There are a thousand ways to obtain intelligence. I didn't care if I had to get in touch with someone if the final objective was to obtain information that was of interest to me. I would have gone to anyone for information. It didn't matter to me whether they were a unit, a particular unit, or formation. All that I was after was seeing if they had anything -- any intelligence in their possession that was of interest to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, if I may just pursue this point, and I think we've got to talk with using common sense here now, why would Mr. Imamovic be concerned about the security of these prisoners of war in the custody of the Arabs, if they were not the responsibility of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is your area of responsibility that sort of puts you in charge of security and other related issues. They were in our area of responsibility, and everything that is in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division should be its responsibility. Should be, as I say. Whether it is or, in fact, not, well, that's a different kettle of fish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you to be saying that if a rogue who's not part of the army is just holding people hostage in an area where the 35th Division operates, it then becomes the responsibility of the 35th Division to go out and do civil work and investigate why rogue civilians are misbehaving in the area; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my personal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, I'd like to refer you back to the same passage that we had been discussing. In reference to the briefing of the PK for ObP, you've said that that was -- that that reference is to you. Do you recall what was discussed during this particular briefing that's referenced in this document?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting. There is a list of those who attended up at the top of the page. This was a meeting or a briefing, and Mr. Mrkaljevic probably organised this, simply because there were other units there that were not part of the 35th Division. I don't know why this briefing took place or who needed it, whose purpose it served. I do know that I did not attend this particular meeting. I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But, sir, the passage reads: " ... The briefing of the PK for ObP," so that's the briefing that I'm referring to, and I'm asking you whether you recall what you discussed with Mr. Mrkaljevic during that particular briefing, the one that refers to you.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here "the briefing" and so on. The reference here is to the PK, and then there are the lower-level units, brigades and battalions, and I am sure that I did not attend this meeting. That's 100 per cent, I'm sure of it. I don't have any recollection of that meeting. I know nothing about such a meeting. I really don't know why he convened this meeting, why this meeting was held. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we just be clear on one fact? Is it your position that you never attended the meeting or is it your position that you don't recall? These are two distinct situations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that I did not attend this meeting. I was duty-bound, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on from that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic -- excuse me, Mr. Hajderhodzic, the prisoner that you had encountered in Livade, which -- which army unit was that person a member of?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was from Prnjavor, from the 1st Prnjavor Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which army is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Which army is that, which army is the 1st Prnjavor Light Brigade a part of, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the name of the army was, the army that we faced, whether it was the Army of Republika Srpska, I don't know that, but I personally used a different term for them, and that was actually the same word that they used to describe themselves. I don't know whether their official name was the Army of Republika Srpska or whatever. That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What name did you use which they used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly, the aggressor forces, because from our point of view they were the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did they also call themselves "the aggressive forces?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you just told us that you used the name that they used to call themselves by.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aggressors and Chetniks, and they called themselves "Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They called themselves aggressive Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just Chetniks. They called themselves "Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you called them aggressive Chetniks, and you say you're using the name they called themselves by.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Chetniks" is the term that they used to describe themselves, and I called them either "Chetniks" or "aggressors."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Hajderhodzic, I just want to refer you again specifically to the second-to-last paragraph and the first sentence of that paragraph. Can you read that again carefully to yourself? Now, the reference in that paragraph to the briefing of the PK for ObP, is it your position that you did not attend that particular briefing to which Mr. Mrkaljevic refers?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit 396.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hajderhodzic, we're changing gears here. You had -- you had mentioned that one of the sources of intelligence information was through reconnaissance, and so I'm showing you a document relating to reconnaissance, and I would ask that you read -- if we could scroll down in the English, please. If you could read point 1 to yourself, Mr. Hajderhodzic. And on the English, that carries over onto the second page.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page. Sir, there are references to certain features and reconnaissance of those features. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us how important these particular features were to the military objectives of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: These features were not only important for the BH Army but for the whole population living there. They were extremely important. In particular, two features, Blizna and Paljenik, were extremely important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And now I'm referring to the features Dolac, Blizna, Vis and Paljenik. How difficult was it to reconnoiter these particular features?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Well, in light of the relief, it was very difficult to do so. Paljenik was especially difficult to reconnoiter. But let me start from the first one, Blizna. Blizna is maybe three or four kilometres from the centre of Zavidovici as the crow flies, and from Blizna you can see every single little nook and cranny in the town. You can control the whole town, every little house and every little hidden corner. Blizna was important for the aggressor forces because they could spot for their artillery when they fired on the town, on the factory and so on. And as for Paljenik, Velika Greda, it was a large feature. It was the key that opened up the whole Krivaja Valley. It is a dominant height. On the one side, you can see almost all the way to Zavidovici, and on the other, up until Vozuca in the direction of Banovici, so you have a line of sight to all those areas. But let me go back to Blizna. I forgot to mention that apart from being close to Zavidovici and having a good line of sight, it makes it possible for you to control everything in the direction of Maglaj and Seher. Even parts of Maglaj can be seen from Blizna, and you can control those areas from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, you've actually explained to us the importance of these particular features, and I was just wondering if you could explain why, specifically, they could be difficult to reconnoiter.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I mentioned a little while ago that because of the relief, because of the lay of the land, but I have to first make one thing clear about the separation lines or front lines. The BH Army was in a subordinate position on all front lines, or it held the lower ground, because the aggressor forces held all the dominant elevations, all the dominant hills. So we were always lower than the aggressor, we held a lower ground. So the sight that had to be reconnoitered was overgrown with low bushes, and it was a wooded area, and the slope was about 70 degrees, so it was really very difficult to reconnoiter it. The soil was rocky. You could not move about without being heard. It would be enough for a little rock to get dislodged and the other side would hear you. So these are the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, you've explained the importance of the Paljenik feature and the Blizna feature, and I was wondering if you could explain the military significance of the Dolac feature and the Vis feature.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Dolac, Blizna, well, the reason is to give a more detailed designation to Blizna. But Vis is something else. It's -- it's a site close to Paljenik, and this is an area from which Paljenik could be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. And can you tell us in which operation these particular features were seized by the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: That was the last operation, Farz-95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when was that operation conducted?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I remember the date. I think it was the 9th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a map here that I would like for the witness to mark with the features that he's just discussed, and it's Map 11 from the Court binder, from the map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the -- do you see the locations of Dolac, Blizna, Paljenik and Vis on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Paljenik should be written somewhere here [indicates], Dolac is here [indicates], but Paljenik should be around here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could move the map further to the -- to the right?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Blizna [indicates], this is Blizna [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you circle Blizna and mark a "1" next to it?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you write a little harder, sir, and make a thicker line around it, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Does the feature Dolac appear on this map, sir?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you circle it and mark a "2" next to it?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Does the feature Vis appear on this map, sir? And if we could move the map a little bit to the right. Excuse me, a little to the left, sorry, towards the witness.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Which one is that after 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The feature Vis, sir. And it's referred to as --

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: It's here [indicates] to the left. Could I first mark Paljenik and then go on to find this other elevation, because this is a rather small-scale map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you could mark Paljenik with -- circle Paljenik and mark a "3" next to it.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now if you could find the feature referred to as "Vis."

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if you could mark a "4" next to it.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall -- the document that I'd showed you is dated the 2nd of June, 1995. Do you recall where the enemy lines were located as of that date?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: I remember, of course, approximately, given the time that has passed, but I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you trace out the enemy lines, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes [marks]. This would be it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Can you mark on which side the ABiH had its strength? On which side of the line was the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: That would be to our left, all the way up to here [indicates], including the town of Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you mark that with an "X"?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you mark, with another "X," the area where the VRS was located? And I'd like you to circle the other "X" where the VRS was. On which side of the line was the VRS?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: That would be on this side [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Just mark that and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this map be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 555.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P02444. And if we could go to page 6 of the English version of the document and page 3 of the B/C/S version of the document. And if we could scroll down on the B/C/S version of the document -- or, excuse me, the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, whose initials -- the initials "HI," to whom do they belong?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: That's my initials, "HI."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And whose signature appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And Mr. Hasanagic's name appears on the document, though; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZUDIN HAJDERHODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S.
